{"stories":{"featured":[{"story_id":197120,"story_date":1793717007,"slug":"moses-boyd-songs-for-sinners-review","description":"A conversation that proves why Moses Boyd is so delightfully hard to pin down.","full_text":"“Wait…so this is jazz?” my wife said, bewilderment in her voice, as “Say Yeah”—the fourth track on “Songs For Sinners”—played in our car. “That’s not how I would have described this.”

“How would you have described it?” I asked, always curious about her opinion on this stuff; she’s no expert, but she’s put up with my listening habits for 20 years and she pays close attention.

“Well, it’s actually a lot of things. This track is definitely very gospel, with the piano and organ, the choir, and this lady vocalist working it out. But there’s also this serious dance-club drum groove: that heavy stomp. And a kind of lilt, and some hand percussion, and this folk-song melody—it sounds a little bit Afro-Caribbean.”

“You’ve got a good ear,” I said. “This is a drummer named Moses Boyd, and he’s a major jazz guy in London. The London jazz scene is really an outgrowth of the EDM scene, which is why you’re hearing those grooves.”

“But not here.” She gestured toward the speaker, now playing the track “Criticise.” “There’s jazz in the drums here, which this singer really brings out, too. But there’s also a lot of funk, and maybe some reggae. That Afro-Caribbean feeling again.”

“Well, that’s the other thing about the London scene,” I said. “It’s very tuned into the African-British diaspora: like they’re decolonizing jazz. Moses Boyd’s mother is Jamaican, so reggae is always a part of the mix for him. But his family is also deeply religious, which means gospel is huge. The album as a whole is really a tribute to that foundation.”

“And this singer—her name is Amber-Simone—I wouldn’t generally call her a jazz singer. More like soul and R&B.”

“Oh, I totally hear that,” my wife said. “But that delivery is so smooth—it’s kind of like Sade, R&B with that chill, jazzy vibe to it. Maybe it’s the London-ness of it that I’m hearing.”

“Speaking of that Sade vibe, check this out,” I said, flipping to “War.” “This is a neo-soul singer named Raelle.”

“Yes! Exactly,” my wife said, grinning and nodding her head to Raelle’s quietly impassioned testimony.

“But then there’s this,” I added, going to “It Is Well.” “First, an a cappella gospel choir, singing basically a spiritual…” We listened. “Then this glitchy electro stuff…then, finally, Fender Rhodes and bebop sax lines on top of all of that.”

“So then is this what you’d call ‘spiritual jazz’?” she asked. (She really has been paying attention.)

“Definitely,” I said. “But not the usual John Coltrane/Pharoah Sanders kind. This is its own animal—with a lot of London-ness, like you said. But just in case you doubted it, at the beginning of the first track, ‘Precious,’ Moses has the saxophone sneak in a quote from a Duke Ellington tune called ‘Come Sunday’ that’s really the granddaddy of spiritual jazz.”

“Really clever,” my wife said. “And really cool. I like it.” She has excellent taste.

–Michael J. Instead, ambient and New Age ruminations sprawl with celestial curiosity, while pre-Hispanic instruments and cinematic field recordings ground the secrets of the universe in our own verdant home-world. The result is a fascinating dialogue between ancient wisdom and Space-Age zeal, with just enough rock grooves for the body to pick up wherever your intellectual journey peters out.

Curated by the Mexican journalist Carlos “Tropicaza” Icaza and Mark “Frosty” McNeill of the Seattle label Light in the Attic, the two-part series collects 25 pieces by artists unified in their “search for a Mexican musical root.” Similar to Bolivia’s jazz new wave and Argentina’s electronic infancy, these works are contextualized as a countercultural response to the repression of rock ‘n’ roll and Mexican youth movements of the ‘60s and ‘70s. The founding of the Mexico City artist market, El Chopo, in 1980, as well as the emergence of DIY labels that challenged traditional means of music creation and distribution, fostered a new generation of sound artists that appropriated and subverted the minimalism and electroacoustic trends of the academic art world with evocative indigenous techniques.

Volume 1 kicks off with “Viento De Lluvia” by Antonio Zepeda and Eugenio Toussaint, and “Sazilakab” by Jorge Reyes, pieces that layer wind chimes, rainsticks, the clay flute known as tlapitzalli, and even Afro-diasporic kalimba. In conjunction with atmospheric electronic production, the composers conceive a world where technology and nature can coexist in harmony, later populated by the flowing waters of Tito’s “Anáhuac” and the chirping synthesized birds of Antonio Russek’s “La Trama de la Vida.”

The album’s second act pivots from eco-meditations into an abstract rock opera, where Luis Pérez’s 15-minute odyssey “Suite Al Culto Solar” unfolds over a Santana-esque mix of psychedelic guitars and tropical percussion. Xavier Zetina’s “Bahía Azteca” swerves into new wave territory with drum machines and vaporous synths, while the bouncy and unexpectedly catchy “La Pirámide” taps into the hitmaking abilities of Jorge García Castil and his trailblazing bands Los Locos del Ritmo and Mister Loco.

Tribu’s New Age pseudo-ballad “Cantar de la Dualidad (Ometekuikatl)” kicks off A La Altura’s final and most contemplative chapter, verbalizing the tension between existence and nothingness that has been a universal building block since the Big Bang. We’re allowed to stew in the mysteries of everything on the final tracks, “Último Encuentro” and “Ascenso,” where echoes of Vangelis and Philip Glass offer a glimmer of familiarity as we venture into the unknown. The album’s remarkable balance of avant-garde experiments and accessible listening even translates to the cover art by Eduardo Terrazas, best known for designing the iconic logo for the 1968 Mexico Olympics, but whose decades-long exploration of cosmic geometry perfectly captures the compilation’s mix of stargazing and terrestrial awe.
